the harmonised covariate set and we report them as negative results. Fitting on
the raw prevalence scale rather than the clamped logit scale, which had been
expected to help because 8 of 24 cells have more than 40% of districts observed
at exactly zero prevalence, gave −0.020 mean Spearman (better in 2 of 4).
Adding district centroid coordinates to the predictor set gave 0.000 (better in
1 of 4); with a top-30 correlation prescreen over 294 predictors, two
coordinate columns rarely survive selection, whereas the exploratory result had
come from a curated 16-variable set in which coordinates were a large share of
the model.

We also directly tested whether the full-mode SuperLearner's 13th candidate
learner, a Gaussian process (`kernlab::gausspr`), was worth its
$O(n^3)$ computational cost, which made the largest pooled LOCO fits
(10,011 and 13,107 rows) effectively non-terminating. Refitting Ghana child
iron — arbitrarily chosen as a representative, well-powered cell — with and
without the Gaussian process in the candidate library gave an identical
binary AUC to 16 decimal places (0.7015504) and a negligible continuous-r
difference (0.2488 vs 0.2540): the Gaussian process received effectively
zero ensemble weight. We therefore dropped it from the full-mode stack
(Methods), retaining the check as a pipeline target rather than removing the
learner on assumption alone.

## Calibration and reliability of binary classifiers

For binary deficiency classifiers, several diagnostic flags emerged
(@tbl-calibration). The Brier skill score was negative — indicating
predictions worse than the no-skill baseline — for 12 of 24
country–outcome combinations, though in most the deficit was small (Brier
skill > −0.04 for 9 of the 12). Post-hoc Platt recalibration (see Methods) eliminated the
negative values entirely: all 24 calibrated classifiers achieved
non-negative Brier skill. Calibration slopes were
strongly inverted
(< 0) for 5 of 24 models — in Gambia, Ghana (×2), Sierra Leone, and Malawi —
particularly at very low prevalence (vitamin A in women, vitamin B12 in
women) where AUC remained high (> 0.7 for two of the five: Ghana women's
vitamin A 0.75, Sierra Leone women's B12 0.75) but Brier skill was near zero.
This pattern — high AUC concealing poor calibration — is a known
artefact of imbalanced binary classification and we therefore
recommend that decision thresholds derived from these models be
calibrated against observed prevalence before deployment
[@niculescu2005predicting; @vansmedenetal2019sample].

```{r tbl-calibration}
#| tbl-cap: "Binary classifier calibration. Brier skill > 0 indicates information gain over a no-skill baseline. From results/tables/diagnostics_binary.csv."
if (!is.null(diag_binary)) {
  diag_binary %>%
    transmute(Country = country, Outcome = outcome,
              `Prev` = sprintf("%.1f%%", prevalence*100),
              AUC = sprintf("%.2f", roc_auc),
              `Brier skill` = sprintf("%+.3f", brier_skill),
              `Calib slope` = sprintf("%+.2f", calib_slope),
              ECE = sprintf("%.3f", ece)) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE)
}
```

## Honest evaluation: the corrected analysis of record

The metrics in this section are the analysis of record, produced by the
leakage-free corrected (P1–P8) methods described in Methods; the
production-pipeline equivalents elsewhere are retained for comparison.

**Within-country discrimination shrinks under honest cross-validation.**
Replacing random cross-validation and full-data preprocessing with
cluster-blocked and spatial-block folds and strictly in-fold preprocessing
lowers within-country discrimination, confirming that the optimistic design
overstated performance (@tbl-cv-honesty). Across the four primary outcomes the
honest (cluster-block) AUC is typically a few points below the optimistic AUC
and frequently near chance, consistent with the modest area-level signal seen
throughout.

```{r tbl-cv-honesty}
#| tbl-cap: "Within-country binary discrimination (AUC) under optimistic versus honest cross-validation, from the corrected methods (results/tables/corrected/cv_honesty_compare.csv). Honest schemes block folds by survey cluster and by spatial region and confine all preprocessing to the training fold."
if (!is.null(corr_cv)) {
  lab <- c("random CV + full-data preprocessing (optimistic)" = "Optimistic",
           "cluster-block CV"                                 = "Cluster-block (honest)",
           "region/spatial-block CV"                          = "Spatial-block (honest)")
  corr_cv %>%
    mutate(scheme = lab[scheme]) %>%
    filter(!is.na(scheme)) %>%
    select(country, outcome, scheme, auc) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = scheme, values_from = auc) %>%
    arrange(country, outcome) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2,
          col.names = c("Country", "Outcome", "Optimistic",
                        "Cluster-block (honest)", "Spatial-block (honest)"))
}
```

**Out-of-fold calibration.** Recalibrating binary predictions out-of-fold
(rather than in-sample) gives an honest picture of calibration; the in-sample
Platt fit is optimistic by construction (slope forced toward 1). Raw and
out-of-fold-calibrated slopes are reported per outcome in
`results/tables/corrected/calibration_oof_compare.csv`.

**Admin-2 error, separating sampling noise from model error.** A substantial
part of the apparent district-level error is survey sampling noise rather than
model error. After removing the sampling-variance component, the
sampling-adjusted RMSE is the honest measure of how far model predictions sit
from the true district prevalence (@tbl-corr-error).

```{r tbl-corr-error}
#| tbl-cap: "Admin-2 prediction error decomposed into a survey-sampling component and a model component (results/tables/corrected/admin2_error_sampling_adjusted.csv). Naive RMSE is the raw predicted-vs-survey error; the sampling component is what survey noise alone would produce; the adjusted RMSE is the honest model error."
if (!is.null(corr_err)) {
  corr_err %>%
    select(country, outcome, n_admin2, naive_rmse_pp, sampling_rmse_pp,
           adjusted_rmse_pp, pearson_r) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2,
          col.names = c("Country", "Outcome", "n areas", "Naive RMSE (pp)",
                        "Sampling RMSE (pp)", "Adjusted RMSE (pp)", "r"))
}
```

**Decision value for targeting.** Because the operational task is to find the
highest-burden districts, we score how well the predictions concentrate true
burden in the top-ranked districts. Targeting the top 20% of districts by
predicted prevalence reaches more of the true burden than untargeted allocation
(lift > 1) for most outcomes, with the largest lift on the outcomes that have
the most spatial signal (@tbl-decision).

```{r tbl-decision}
#| tbl-cap: "Decision value of district ranking (results/tables/corrected/decision_value.csv). reach@20% is the share of true burden captured by the top 20% of districts ranked by predicted prevalence; lift is that reach divided by the 20% an untargeted allocation would reach; hit-rate@top20 is the share of the predicted top-20% districts that are truly in the top 20%."
if (!is.null(corr_decision)) {
  corr_decision %>%
    select(country, outcome, reach_at_20pct, lift_vs_no_targeting, hit_rate_top20) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2,
          col.names = c("Country", "Outcome", "Reach@20%", "Lift", "Hit-rate@top20"))
}
```

**Prediction intervals are reasonably calibrated.** Split-conformal intervals
attached to each surveyed district achieve empirical held-out coverage close to
the 90% target (range across outcomes typically 0.85–1.00;
`results/tables/corrected/interval_summary.csv`), at the cost of wide intervals
for the noisiest outcomes.

**Per-district trust flags.** Each district is flagged for reliability by three
criteria: whether its covariates fall outside the surveyed training range
(out-of-support), small survey sample, and a wide prediction interval. The
resulting OK-to-use versus do-not-rely labels are in
`results/tables/corrected/trust_flags.csv` and drive the dashboard's certainty
layer; out-of-support is the dominant driver of do-not-rely flags in
unsurveyed districts.

## Prediction under the corrected protocol {#sec-protocol-results}

Re-running every comparison under @sec-protocol changes the conclusions more
than any modelling choice in this paper did.

**The size of the protocol effect.** Our published within-country median rank
correlation of 0.058 rested on a single random division of the districts.
Replicated ten times under the identical protocol, the median is **0.217**
(IQR 0.146-0.289); exhaustive leave-one-region-out gives **0.235**. The
published figure was a low draw, not a measurement. Separately, the comparison
the models appeared to lose was against a regional mean computed from the scored
district's own respondents; scored symmetrically, that baseline achieves
r **0.076** and the covariate model **0.156**. Neither correction involved new
data or a new model.

**Within a surveyed country, covariates beat the honest survey baseline.**
Against a jackknifed regional mean — the only sub-national alternative a
programme actually has — the covariate model attains rank correlation
**0.398** against **0.320** on the biomarker concentration, and **0.286**
against **0.193** on deficiency prevalence, in-fill. Under region
extrapolation the margin widens on prevalence (**0.268** against **-0.107**),
because a regional mean has nothing to say about a region it has not seen.

**Geography alone does most of the within-country work.** A covariate-free
spatial smoother scores **0.391** where the full covariate model scores
**0.398**. This replicates our published finding and we do not retract it: inside
a surveyed country, most of what the covariates supply is a smooth surface that
neighbouring-district information already provides. The covariates earn their
place in two specific situations — against a survey-derived baseline once that
baseline is made information-symmetric, and where there is no survey to smooth
from at all.

**Rank transports across borders; level does not.** Under leave-one-country-out,
district rankings transport with a mean Spearman of **0.26** over the 22
evaluable country-outcome combinations for the zero-tuning domain index (17
positive; the penalised domain fit gives 0.24 with 21 positive) and **0.37**
(22 positive) for an index built from the climate and soil domains alone. At
the first sub-national tier (regions, or Malawi's districts) the same 22
combinations give a mean Spearman of **0.30** (17 positive), and **0.45** (20
positive) for the climate-and-soil index; a country-block permutation null,
which keeps the correlation between outcomes within a country, has a 95th
percentile of 0.16 for the regional mean and 0.08 for the district mean, so
the means are far outside chance while counts of positive cells are not (no
transport at all yields 15–16 of 22 positive five percent of the time). An earlier draft of this section carried
a regional figure of 0.50–0.56 over 12 combinations; that figure rested on
three countries, because a spelling mismatch in the population file had
dropped Sierra Leone from every population-joined run, and it is withdrawn.
Absolute prevalence levels do not
transport, consistent with the biomarker level offsets between surveys reported
in @sec-zscore. The transportable product is therefore a ranked priority list,
not a prevalence map. We note one negative: burden-weighted targeting lift under
transport is **1.007** across 12 evaluable cells, better than random in only 5,
so the transport claim is about ordering and should not be restated as a
targeting gain.

**Capacity is not the binding constraint; it is a liability.** The zero-tuning
domain index outperforms elastic net over all 451 predictors by up to **0.38**,
and the 451-column fit turns *negative* under region extrapolation. With 14-87
units, a penalised regression over hundreds of correlated columns fits the
country it was trained in.

**In programme terms.** Visiting the worst-ranked fifth of districts reaches
**26%** more national deficiency burden than the same effort guided by the
survey's own regional averages, which are themselves no better than choosing
districts at random (in-fill lift 1.20 for the model, 0.95 for regional
averages, against an oracle ceiling of 2.43). For Malawi child iron, the
selected districts carry **43.1%** deficiency against **26.3%** nationally and
hold **48.7%** of the national burden in children.

**What tracks which nutrient.** Because no per-cell test of 451 predictors can
have usable power at these sample sizes (@sec-fdr), we report cross-country
replication of sign. @tbl-nutrient-signal lists, for each outcome, the
indicators with the strongest pooled association that also point the same way in
every country in which they are measured.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nutrient-signal
#| tbl-cap: "Indicators most strongly associated with each outcome that also
#|   replicate in sign across all contributing countries. Strength is a pooled
#|   random-effects z across countries; 'agree' is the number of countries in
#|   which the indicator points the same way, out of those measuring it.
#|   Produced by scripts/signal_probes/p4_admin1_continuous_scan.R."
#| echo: false
f <- here::here("results", "tables", "signal_probes",
                "p4_admin1_continuous_predictors.csv")
if (file.exists(f)) {
  d <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  keep_g <- c("child_vitA", "child_iron", "women_iron", "women_vitA", "women_b12")
  d <- d[d$sign_agree >= d$k_countries & d$k_countries >= 3 &
           d$group %in% keep_g, ]
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(d, d$group), function(g) {
    g <- g[order(-abs(g$meta_z)), ]
    utils::head(g, 3)
  }))
  out <- data.frame(
    Outcome   = d$group,
    Indicator = d$predictor,
    Domain    = d$domain,
    Strength  = round(d$meta_z, 2),
    Direction = ifelse(d$mu > 0, "more deficiency", "less deficiency"),
    Agree     = paste0(d$sign_agree, "/", d$k_countries))
  knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllrlc")
} else {
  cat("Signal scan not available; run scripts/signal_probes/p4_admin1_continuous_scan.R.")
}
```

**Dense signal where the sparse screen found none.** The omnibus test of
@sec-fdr, powered against many small effects, rejects the no-association null in
the majority of cells, and the per-nutrient sign-replication results are given in
@tbl-nutrient-signal. The signal is real, distributed across many indicators, and
nutrient-specific; it is not concentrated in a few predictors that a sparse
screen could isolate at this sample size.

# Discussion

## Summary

We harmonised individual-level biomarker measurements from four sub-Saharan
African DHS (three West African plus Malawi) to evaluate whether models built on
remotely sensed and survey-derived proxies can reproduce admin-2 micronutrient
deficiency prevalence and national prevalence. An internal audit of an earlier
version of this manuscript found that several of its headline conclusions were
determined by the evaluation design rather than by the data, so the findings
below are those that survive re-analysis under a pre-specified protocol
(@sec-protocol). Five have programmatic significance.

**First, evaluation design dominated modelling choice.** No change to any model
in this paper moved a result as much as three changes to how results were
scored. Replicating a single random split moved a headline within-country
correlation from 0.058 to 0.217. Making a survey-derived baseline
information-symmetric with the model — it had been computed from the scored
district's own respondents — moved the same comparison from a loss to a win
(0.156 against 0.076). Recognising that a permutation screen could not clear its
own multiplicity threshold at the resolution used removed a reported null
finding entirely. Two further corrections ran against us: the reliability
ceiling we used to argue admin-2 was unresolvable was biased low by roughly a
factor of 4.7, and the regional-anchoring gain we reported as the single most
valuable design choice disappears under a jackknifed control. We report all five
because a reader has no way to tell, from a manuscript, which conclusions were
protocol artifacts and which were measurements.

**Second, proxy indicators carry replicated, nutrient-specific signal — but it
is not individual-level biology.** Under cross-country sign replication, the
appropriate evidence standard when no per-cell test of 451 predictors can have
power at 14–87 districts, the associations replicate in direction across all
four surveys while several run *opposite* to what individual nutrition predicts:
district legume consumption tracks more child vitamin A deficiency, and cattle
ownership more child iron deficiency. Together with cereal cropping, warm night
temperatures and soil heterogeneity, the replicated axis is best read as rural
subsistence agro-ecology — area-level markers of deficient districts rather than
exposures to intervene on. The exception is women's vitamin A, which tracks
district child wasting and, inversely, rainfall, and is interpretable as stated.
No malaria burden indicator replicated against any outcome.

**Third, covariate models beat the honest survey baseline within a country, but
geography does most of the work.** Against a jackknifed regional mean the
covariate model attains rank correlation 0.398 versus 0.320 on the biomarker and
0.286 versus 0.193 on prevalence. A covariate-free spatial smoother, however,
scores 0.391 where the full covariate model scores 0.398 — our published finding
on this point replicates and we do not retract it. The covariates earn their
complexity against a survey-derived baseline and where no survey exists to
smooth from, not as a general improvement on spatial smoothing.

**Fourth, rank transports across borders and level does not.** District rankings
transport under leave-one-country-out with a mean Spearman of 0.26 over 22
combinations (0.37 for the climate-and-soil index, positive in all 22), and
regional rankings with 0.30 (0.45 for climate and soil), against permutation
nulls whose 95th percentiles are 0.08 and 0.16; absolute prevalence does not,
consistent with the biomarker level offsets
between surveys documented in @sec-zscore. The transportable deliverable is a
ranked priority list. We note against ourselves that burden-weighted targeting
lift under transport is 1.007 across 12 cells, so the transport result should not
be restated as a targeting gain — that claim holds in-fill (lift 1.20 against
0.95 for regional survey averages), not across borders.

**Fifth, capacity is a liability at this sample size.** A zero-tuning index over
18 domain summaries beats elastic net over all 451 predictors by up to 0.38, and
the 451-column fit turns negative under region extrapolation. National-level
aggregation, meanwhile, remains accurate throughout (24 of 24 country-outcome
predictions within the survey's 95% CI) and is the deliverable best supported by
the evidence where a district ranking is not required.

## The aggregation problem and "fit at the unit of deliverable"

The mechanism by which individual-level predictions degrade upon
aggregation merits explicit treatment. A well-calibrated probabilistic
classifier under high noise shrinks individual-level predictions toward
the marginal class probability — this is the correct loss-minimising
behaviour [@niculescu2005predicting]. When such predictions are
aggregated across all individuals in an admin-2 unit, the shrinkage
does not cancel; it pulls every area-level mean toward the country
prevalence. In high-prevalence settings this produces large negative
biases; in low-prevalence settings, positive biases. Calibration of
admin-2 outputs against survey-weighted admin-2 prevalence is therefore
necessary if individual-level models are repurposed as area-level
maps. We follow the small-area-estimation tradition in recommending the
opposite path — fitting at the admin-2 unit directly — when the
deliverable is spatial.

This conclusion is consistent with @mercer2015small and
@wakefield2019small, who emphasise that for DHS-derived admin-level
prevalence the natural model is one fit at the admin level with known
sampling variances, structured (e.g., ICAR or BYM2) random effects,
and auxiliary covariates. Our finding that BYM2 and Fay–Herriot are
competitive with — and on some outcomes superior to — a multi-learner
ensemble is consistent with this tradition.

## Why does the SuperLearner sometimes underperform?

The most striking single result is the child-iron Sierra Leone LOCO case,
where the SuperLearner produces anti-predictive ranking (r = −0.125, MAE
20.0 pp) while a beta regression on the same covariates achieves r = 0.466
at a fraction of the absolute error (MAE 3.4 pp) — and every other linear
comparator we tested (GLM, quasi-binomial, penalised regression) was also
anti-predictive on this cell, so the ensemble's failure is not simply "any
simpler model would have done better." We interpret this as a
model-selection failure specific to the ensemble: with only 14 admin-2 areas
in the held-out set and roughly 150 covariates, the cross-validated risk
estimator within the ensemble has high variance, and the cv-selected learner
appears to have over-fit to a non-transportable feature pattern that a
correctly-specified beta regression, respecting the outcome's bounded
[0, 1] support, avoided.

This suggests that ensemble methods should be benchmarked against
parsimonious alternatives — including distribution-appropriate ones, not
only linear-Gaussian baselines — whenever the test set is small or the
target population is meaningfully outside the training distribution. Full
mode of our pipeline (the 12-learner SuperLearner across 206 admin-2 units
and five outcomes) took several hours end to end (2026-08 rebuild: 831
targets, 0 errors); a single comparator model such as beta regression
fits in seconds. Across the 16 LOCO cells evaluated in @tbl-benchmarks, that
cost was justified on none.

## Implications for programming

The national-level estimates in this study are, on present evidence, the
most defensible deliverable for programming: 24 of 24 country–outcome
national predictions fell inside the survey's own confidence interval.
Admin-2 deficiency maps derived from the same models are, at best,
interpretable as *relative ranking* tools within a country with biomarker
data — useful for prioritising districts within a national-level
intervention — but should be published alongside their reliability ceiling
(@sec-ceiling), since roughly a sixth of country–outcome cells have no
detectable admin-2 signal at all and should not be mapped as if they did.
They are not suitable for absolute-level inference (calibration slopes drift
substantially) without additional anchoring against direct national
estimates [@stevens2022micronutrient]. For an unsurveyed country, our
results suggest that LOCO-based predictions should be treated as coarse risk
triage at most, benchmarked against a national-mean null and a
covariate-free spatial smoother before any claim of added value, and used
only within the same broad agroecological region as the training set.

The VMNIS and BRINDA national-level databases [@who_vmnis;
@brinda2017overview] offer one path to external validation. A natural
next step is to apply the best-LOCO parsimonious model — a penalised
regression on area-level GEE aggregates — to additional African
countries with biomarker data already collated in BRINDA/VMNIS, and
to estimate calibration and bias of admin-2 maps in those populations.
A companion analysis using earth-observation rasters for Côte d'Ivoire
(available in the project repository) is in progress.

## Limitations

Our sample comprises four sub-Saharan African countries — three in West
Africa plus Malawi — so the rest of East, Central, and Southern Africa is
unrepresented. Because the predictors are resolved at admin-2, the
effective sample size for area-level models is the
number of polygons (14–90 per country) rather than the underlying
individuals, which limits the degrees of freedom for both within- and
cross-country fitting and makes naively-computed within-country
cross-validated correlations an optimistic bound in the absence of an
explicit reliability ceiling (most acutely for Sierra Leone, with only 14
polygons) — a limitation we address directly by reporting r_max alongside
every correlation (@sec-ceiling), but the ceiling estimate itself carries
uncertainty from the small number of respondents per district. We did not
formally quantify the contribution of survey design weights to admin-2
prevalence estimates; assuming a fixed design-effect of 1.5 (DHS-typical) is
an approximation, and we separately note that DHS sample weights were found
to sit on inconsistent numeric scales across countries in our cohort (e.g.
a median in the hundreds of thousands in one survey against below 1 in
another), which is immaterial for weighted means but would bias any
downstream use of the weights as a precision measure. The cross-country
common-vocabulary covariate set is 294 variables assembled from every admin-2
source available (@sec-predictors); predictors not present in all four
countries were excluded, and three domains — food security, food prices and
accessibility — contribute nothing to the pooled models because no single
column name is common to all four, a limitation of the strict-intersection
policy rather than of the underlying data.

Three further limitations arise from analyses added after peer review. First,
inflammation adjustment is harmonised across countries for vitamin A but not
for iron, which retains each survey's native adjustment (Thurnham, BRINDA
regression, or a log-scale regression correction); the raw components for a
uniform adjustment exist in all four surveys, and harmonising them did not
alter cross-country transport in our testing, but the asymmetry remains.
Second, several biomarkers collected in these surveys are unused, most
consequentially soluble transferrin receptor, which is available in all four
countries and is substantially less inflammation-sensitive than ferritin.
Third, all outcomes are modelled as binaries at a cutoff; for the rarest
outcomes this discards most of the available information — Malawi women's
vitamin A comprises 11 events in 836 respondents — and we show elsewhere that
the same outcome behaves very differently at admin-1, where cases accumulate.
Finally,
our raw binary classifiers' calibration diagnostics
flagged roughly half of country–outcome cells with a calibration slope well
below 1 (median 0.51 before correction); post-hoc recalibration corrects
this, but the underlying discrimination at very low prevalence remains weak
(several AUCs near 0.5, and one cell — Malawi child zinc, AUC 0.448 — below
chance) and these outcomes should be treated as exploratory.

## External validation pathway

The findings presented here are based on a largely West African LOCO panel
(three West African countries plus Malawi) and a single external held-out
country (Côte d'Ivoire). We have
prepared a multi-source national-level benchmark to evaluate future
expansions of the model to East and Southern Africa, comprising: (i) the
Kenya National Micronutrient Survey 2011 [@knms2011], which provides
nationally-representative biomarker prevalence for vitamin A, iron,
zinc, folate, B12 and iodine across pre-school children, school-age
children, pregnant women, non-pregnant women, and men; (ii) modelled
WHO/UNICEF joint anaemia prevalence estimates for all eight focus
countries, retrieved via the WHO Global Health Observatory API; and
(iii) WHO Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS)
historical survey-level prevalence for the same eight countries, from
the latest publicly-released long-format dump. The Stevens et al. 2022
*Lancet Global Health* pooled posterior estimates [@stevens2022micronutrient] are the
natural comparator for our national-level predictions; however, the
country-level Bayesian posteriors are not publicly released, only the
22 input surveys used to fit the model, and none of our cohort countries
are among them. The full assembled benchmark is in
`results/external/{vmnis_national,who_anaemia_country,knms2011_national_summary,kenya_national_benchmark}.csv`.

Concrete next-step datasets, each requiring a Data Use Agreement
with the originating ministry, would substantially expand the LOCO panel
beyond West Africa: the Kenya National Micronutrient Survey (KNMS 2011)
and the Ethiopia National Micronutrient Survey 2016, both of which
include the full vitamin A / iron / zinc / folate / B12 / iodine biomarker
panel collected under the BRINDA inflammation-adjustment framework, making
harmonisation with our four training countries straightforward. We
attempted to add Tanzania via the 2010 TDHS but withdrew it (Methods); the
2023 Tanzania DHS, which we understand uses serum rather than
dried-blood-spot vitamin-A assessment, is a better-supported candidate once
its data become accessible. As a lighter-weight alternative for iron, the
most recent DHS rounds with haemoglobin biomarker (Kenya DHS 2022, Burkina
Faso DHS 2021) can be added with no further paperwork beyond the user's
existing DHS account, providing iron-deficiency anaemia coverage for two
additional East/Sahelian countries. We
provide country-agnostic ingestion stubs (`R/ingest_new_country.R`,
function `stub_new_country_config()`) for each of these candidates;
once a harmonised survey file lands in `data/IPD/<country>/`, the entire
LOCO, calibration, SHAP, and dashboard pipeline regenerates automatically.

## Future methodological directions

The results above locate the limits of the current approach precisely — a
low reliability ceiling on the admin-2 target itself, transport that fails
on both level and pattern depending on the method, and an ensemble that does
not beat parsimonious SAE baselines or two uninformed nulls — and these
limits motivate several planned extensions. We describe them here as
directions rather than results.

First, **decision-focused estimation.** For programmatic use the relevant target
is rarely the exact prevalence of a district but whether it lies above a
public-health action threshold, and whether the highest-risk districts are
correctly prioritised. Because the SuperLearner's base learners optimise
likelihood or squared-error loss while the ensembling (or discrete-selection)
step may target any criterion [@vanderlaan2007super], the ensemble can be tuned
directly for an aggregate, asymmetric objective — for example maximising recall of
the truly high-risk areas (top-quantile or above-threshold) subject to a bounded
false-positive rate. This reframes the deliverable toward the ranking signal that,
as shown above, transports more reliably than absolute level, and is
statistically less demanding than level estimation.

Second, **anchoring — but to regions, not to a nation.** An earlier version of
this paper proposed level recalibration against a known or historical national
value (e.g. from VMNIS or the BRINDA pooled analyses
[@who_vmnis; @brinda2017overview]) as a promising direction. We have since tested
it and report the result rather than the proposal. Anchoring to *regional*
design-based totals is the single most valuable step we found (@sec-anchoring);
anchoring to a *national* total is not, and a national level that must itself be
predicted is worse than no anchor at all (@sec-national-composition). The
productive version of this direction is therefore the acquisition of
regional-level anchors — a survey design question rather than a modelling one —
and the useful methodological work lies in how few regions, and how thinly
sampled, an anchor set can be before the gain disappears.

Third, **borrowing strength across co-occurring deficiencies.** The micronutrient
outcomes are biologically correlated but were modelled independently here.
Modelling them jointly through a forward factorisation of their conditional
density — predicting the most-informative outcome first (iron, measured in all
four countries) and supplying predicted upstream deficiencies, with
missing-indicator encoding and imputation, as covariates for subsequent outcomes
— is a standard route to exploiting that covariance and may stabilise the
data-poorest outcomes (zinc, B12). We expect within-country gains to exceed
transport gains, since transported upstream predictions themselves carry error.

Fourth, **inference and value-of-information.** Valid uncertainty on the aggregate
deliverable (national or admin-level prevalence) — via cross-validated
loss-based inference, conformal prediction intervals, or the area-resampling
bootstrap already reported — enables a complementary product that is robust to the
data being imperfect: a value-of-information map that ranks candidate survey
locations by the product of predicted risk and predicted uncertainty, identifying
where a new biomarker survey would be most informative. For a field constrained by
the cost and rarity of biomarker measurement, guiding *where to measure next* may
be as valuable as the prevalence estimates themselves.

Finally, the most direct route to a higher reliability ceiling is to raise
the number of biomarker measurements each admin-2 estimate is built from —
pooling survey rounds within a country, modelling at admin-1 where the
survey design actually supports it, or borrowing strength across the
biologically-correlated outcomes above — rather than adding learners to the
ensemble, since @sec-ceiling shows the individual-level model already
captures most of what the current data can support. The most
consequential validation step remains to re-run the entire methodology on
anaemia (haemoglobin), which is measured in nearly every sub-Saharan African
DHS at large sample size: a trusted, abundant outcome would separate
methodological limitations from the disputed comparability of the
micronutrient biomarkers themselves, and would expand the cross-country
panel far beyond the four countries available here.

## Conclusions

Proxy indicators carry replicated, nutrient-specific signal for subnational
micronutrient deficiency status, and several of the negative findings we
previously reported were artifacts of evaluation design rather than properties
of the data. A published within-country correlation of 0.058 was a single
high-variance draw and is 0.217 when replicated; a benchmark the models appeared
to lose to had been computed from the scored district's own respondents; a screen
reported as finding nothing could not have found anything at any effect size;
and the reliability ceiling used to argue that admin-2 was unresolvable was
biased low by about a factor of 4.7. Corrections ran in both directions: the
regional-anchoring gain we reported as the single most valuable design choice
does not survive a jackknifed control, and the finding that a covariate-free
spatial smoother matches the full covariate set within a surveyed country
replicates and stands.

Under the corrected protocol, covariate models beat an information-matched
survey baseline in both within-country estimands, and district rankings
transport to unsurveyed countries with a mean rank correlation of 0.26 (0.37
from climate and soil alone; regional rankings 0.30 and 0.45) while
absolute levels do not. The defensible deliverable is therefore a ranked district priority list
rather than a prevalence map, and it is worth about a quarter more deficiency
burden reached, per unit of programme effort, than the survey's own regional
averages. Within a surveyed country, however, geography alone supplies most of
the attainable accuracy, and the covariates are worth their complexity mainly
where no survey exists to smooth from. Model capacity is not the binding
constraint: a zero-tuning index over 18 domain summaries beats a penalised
regression over 451 predictors, which turns negative when asked to extrapolate
to an unseen region.

For the field, the transferable result is procedural. We recommend that studies
of this kind name the estimand they are evaluating, since in-fill, region
extrapolation and country transport have materially different answers and are
routinely reported interchangeably; state what information the comparison
baseline was permitted to see, and jackknife any baseline derived from the same
survey; replicate every random division of the data and report the spread rather
than a single value; and demonstrate that each significance screen could have
detected an effect had one been present. Applied to our own work, these four
conditions reversed several conclusions, and we would not have identified any of
them from the modelling results alone.
